scoreNote: Between Adequate and Strong (4.5): a recommendation-appropriate response that shows in most circumstances the policy is unfair and distorting, then concedes the case for accountability and offers fairer measures; clear, if treading familiar ground.

sentences.text: It seems only fair to pay the best teachers the most, and a student's performance looks like an objective measure of who the best teachers are.
The recommendation would therefore tie teachers' salaries to the academic performance of their students.

Although the recommendation is appealing, in most circumstances adopting it would do more harm than good, because student performance is shaped by far more than the teacher, and rewarding it directly corrupts teaching itself.

sections.role: Body — Results are not the teacher's alone

sentences.text: First, in the circumstances most teachers actually work in, student results reflect forces well beyond their control.
Home life, health, language, poverty, and prior schooling shape test scores at least as much as anything that happens in class.
A gifted teacher in a poor school may lift her students enormously and still see lower scores than a weaker teacher whose pupils arrive already privileged and prepared.
To pay the first teacher less would reward circumstance over skill, the precise unfairness the policy claims to cure.
Where results depend largely on a student's background, scoring teachers by those results is neither fair nor accurate.
Two teachers of equal skill, handed unequal classes, will post unequal scores through no fault of their own.
It would judge the gardener by the weather as much as by the gardening.
Moreover, in almost any school the policy would corrupt the teaching it means to improve.
Teachers paid by test scores have every incentive to teach narrowly to the test, drill memorization, and quietly avoid the weakest students.
The richest parts of education — curiosity, creativity, and character — produce nothing a standardized test records, and so would be the first to be dropped.
Over time the policy would also drive the best teachers away from the struggling schools that need them most, since no one will accept lower pay for harder work.
A measure becomes worthless the moment people start gaming it, and tying livelihoods to scores guarantees they will.
Pay people for test numbers, and test numbers, not learning, are what you will get.
The circumstances in which this policy improves teaching are rare; the ones in which it deforms teaching are everywhere.
However, the recommendation does respond to a legitimate concern.
Teachers, like anyone, should be accountable for whether their students actually learn, and a school cannot ignore results entirely.

But there are far better measures than raw scores — how much a teacher improves her students over a year, classroom observation, and peer and parent feedback — that reward real effectiveness without the distortions.
These reward what teachers genuinely control rather than the luck of which students they happened to be given.
Real accountability asks how far students travelled, not merely where they happened to end up.
Accountability is a reason to judge teaching carefully, not to price it by a single number.
In conclusion, in nearly all realistic circumstances, basing teachers' salaries on student performance would do harm.
Because results depend on forces no teacher commands and the policy corrupts the teaching it rewards, a wiser system holds teachers accountable by fairer measures.
Pay teachers for the quality of their teaching, not for the accident of which students walk through the door.
